scope: Every English gloss, full usage paragraph and listed pattern in this range was individually read. Seven flagged entries also had all stored examples inspected. This is not a claim that every example sentence or every morphology in the catalog was individually verified against a dictionary.

findings.finding: The selected meaning is divide/apportion, and isc:true correctly yields ripartisco. aux:both also accepts sono ripartito, which belongs to leave again, not this transitive selected sense.
findings.recommendation: Use avere in the selected lesson sense; keep restart/depart-again as a distinct reference sense.
findings.resolution: Source aux corrected to avere for the selected apportion sense; compiled file awaits coordinated rebuild.

findings.finding: Generic past targets accept both inferito and inferto for the selected infer/deduce meaning. The stored usage correctly distinguishes inferito (deduce) from inferto (inflict).
findings.recommendation: For the taught deduce sense accept inferito; reserve inferto and infersi for an explicitly selected inflict sense and compatible context.

findings.finding: The lesson currently builds personal forms such as mi addico and ti addici for be fitting, although this use has third-person singular/plural subjects. Its source note also overstates absence of compounds: Treccani labels addetto compounds rare.
findings.recommendation: Teach third-person forms in actual thing/behavior subjects. Suppress personal six-person and formal-address drills in this sense. Describe compounds as rare rather than impossible.
findings.resolution: Source rarity wording corrected. Lesson person-scope restriction delegated to lesson-content owner.

findings.finding: The lesson makes io prudo / tu prudi targets although body parts are the subjects in the taught itch sense.
findings.recommendation: Use third-person singular/plural with explicit body-part subjects; the person feeling the itch is an indirect object.

findings.finding: Six personal forms and a polite-addressee target are generated for rules/laws being in force. The selected usage is almost exclusively third-person.
findings.recommendation: Teach third-person law/rule subjects; do not require formal-you morphology for this sense.

findings.finding: Engine/lesson accept ho ostato, while Treccani excludes past participle, compound tenses and passato remoto. Source says only third person, but Treccani lists io osto, so this must be a selected-usage teaching restriction rather than a universal ban.
findings.recommendation: Suppress unavailable compound/remoto teaching and retain a note on the usual nulla osta construction without declaring all personal forms impossible.
findings.resolution: Source personal-form wording corrected. Missing compound/remoto masking delegated to root/lesson-content owner.

findings.finding: Source says no other forms are in use beyond the infinitive. Treccani explicitly allows some present forms, including delinquo, while infinitive and substantive participle are much more common.
findings.recommendation: Explain limited modern use and teach the useful expressions; do not claim present forms are impossible or require a complete normal paradigm.
findings.resolution: Source prose corrected using cited dictionary; compiled file awaits coordinated rebuild.

findings.finding: Source prose says always with per, but stored patterns include propendere a fare. Treccani supports both per + option and a + infinitive.
findings.recommendation: Replace always with per by a sense-sensitive explanation covering both constructions.
findings.resolution: Source prose corrected using cited dictionary; compiled file awaits coordinated rebuild.

findings.finding: Stored usage emphasizes impersonal or third-person subject types. Generated six-person form tables and formal-address questions can misrepresent the selected sense even if a rare personal morphology is possible.
findings.recommendation: Review subject-role eligibility separately from morphological existence; use exact existing contexts and explicit thing/event subjects, avoiding unsupported personal scenes.

findings.finding: Source usage explicitly warns that forms are absent, rare, replaced by another expression, or restricted to particular tenses. Most unavailable participles are already marked missing by the engine; rarity is not uniformly represented as teaching metadata.
findings.recommendation: Keep unavailable forms out of assessment; preserve usage guidance and avoid making rare literary forms a mandatory daily-use lesson.

findings.finding: These are lexical idioms with fixed clitics and often required complements, not automatically compositional reflexives. Bare forms alone do not teach their intended use.
findings.recommendation: Keep progressive construction drills guarded until complete sense-specific scenes are authored; retain fixed pronoun and agreement notes in ordinary reference.

findings.finding: Stored usage distinguishes auxiliary, transitivity, or conjugation across senses. The app data holds one lemma record, so broad form alternatives can cross the selected meaning boundary.
findings.recommendation: Use an explicit lesson sense profile with morphology overrides and selected compatible examples; preserve other meanings in reference.
